renders._yaml:
- component: advanced_viz
  id: mimag_scatter
  title: Bin completeness against contamination
  description: |-
    Each point is a recovered bin: its completeness on the horizontal axis and its contamination on the vertical axis, both estimated by CheckM2, sized by assembly length and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers which bins are good enough to report as genomes.
    How to read: the best bins sit at the bottom right, complete and clean. Bins above the horizontal line are too contaminated for any tier, and bins left of the vertical line are fragmentary. Open the bin table for the lineage and assembly of a bin before trusting it.
    Lines and annotations: the vertical line is 50 percent completeness and the horizontal line 10 percent contamination, the limits of the medium-quality MIMAG tier. The high-quality tier needs more than 90 percent completeness and under 5 percent contamination, together with the 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA genes and at least 18 tRNAs, so a bin can look high quality here and still be medium.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    x_title: Completeness (%)
    y_title: Contamination (%)
    top_n_labels: 0
    legend_pos: bottom
    quadrants:
      x: 50
      y: 10
      labels:
      - Contaminated
      - Contaminated
      - Low quality
      - Medium quality or better
  roles:
    x: completeness
    y: contamination
    label: bin_id
    color: mimag_tier
    size: total_length

- component: advanced_viz
  id: quality_vs_fragmentation
  title: Bin quality against contiguity
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin: the N50 of its contigs on the horizontal axis and its quality score on the vertical axis, sized by assembly length and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers whether the best bins are also the least fragmented.
    How to read: bins in the upper right are complete, clean and contiguous. Bins with a high score but a low N50 are assembled in many pieces, which makes them harder to trust and to annotate.
    Lines and annotations: no line is drawn. The quality score is this table's own summary, completeness minus five times contamination, and is not a published standard.
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    log_x: true
    x_title: N50 (bp)
    y_title: Quality score (completeness minus 5 x contamination)
    top_n_labels: 0
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: n50
    y: quality_score
    label: bin_id
    color: mimag_tier
    size: total_length

- component: advanced_viz
  id: binner_phylum_flow
  title: Assembler, binner and phylum flow
  description: |-
    Each flow is a group of bins: the left column is the assembler, the middle the binning tool and the right the GTDB-Tk phylum, with the width of a flow showing how many bins follow that path. It answers which assembler and binner combinations recover which lineages.
    How to read: a binner with wide flows to many phyla recovers a diverse set of genomes. A phylum reached by one assembler only is a lineage the others missed. Bins GTDB-Tk could not classify have no phylum.
  kind: sankey
  roles:
    steps:
    - assembler
    - binner
    - phylum

- component: advanced_viz
  id: bin_lineage
  title: Bin lineage hierarchy
  description: |-
    Each arc is a taxon of the GTDB-Tk classification of the bins, sized by the assembled length of its bins and coloured by phylum, from domain on the inner ring to genus on the outer. It answers how much of the assembly belongs to which lineages.
    How to read: wide arcs are the lineages that hold most of the recovered sequence. Classification stops at the deepest rank GTDB-Tk could assign, so short branches mean novel or poorly characterised bins.
  kind: sunburst
  config:
    colour_by_rank: phylum
  roles:
    ranks:
    - domain
    - phylum
    - class_name
    - order
    - family
    - genus
    abundance: total_length

- component: figure
  title: Bin quality by binner and MIMAG tier
  description: |-
    Each point is a bin: its quality score, grouped by the binner that recovered it and coloured by MIMAG tier. It answers which binner delivers the best bins.
    How to read: a binner with many high points of a good tier is the most reliable for this data. A binner whose points sit low or fall in the contaminated tier mixes genomes together.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median quality score of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/mag. The score is this table's own summary, completeness minus five times contamination, and is not a published standard.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  visu_type: strip
  dict_kwargs:
    x: binner
    y: quality_score
    color: mimag_tier
    stripmode: group
    labels:
      binner: Binner
      quality_score: Quality score (completeness minus 5 x contamination)
      mimag_tier: MIMAG tier
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: quality_score

- component: card
  id: mimag_donut
  title: Bins recovered
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct bins and the ring splits them by MIMAG tier. It answers how many of the recovered genomes reach each quality level.
    How to read: a ring mostly in the high and medium tiers means a successful binning. A large contaminated share points at binners mixing organisms.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  column: bin_id
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: mimag_tier
  caption: bins, by MIMAG tier

- component: card
  title: Bin completeness
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median completeness of the bins, as estimated by CheckM2, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much of a genome a typical bin holds.
    How to read: a median above 50 percent means most bins are at least medium quality on this criterion. A long lower tail marks fragmentary bins.
    Lines and annotations: the MIMAG standard asks for at least 50 percent completeness for a medium-quality bin and more than 90 percent for a high-quality one.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  column: completeness
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Bin contamination
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median contamination of the bins, as estimated by CheckM2, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how much foreign sequence a typical bin carries.
    How to read: low medians with a short tail mean clean bins. A long upper tail marks bins that mix genomes.
    Lines and annotations: the MIMAG standard allows under 10 percent contamination for a medium-quality bin and under 5 percent for a high-quality one.
    Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28787424/
  column: contamination
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Bin size
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median assembled length of the bins in base pairs, and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how large a typical recovered genome is.
    How to read: very small bins are incomplete genomes, and very large ones may combine several organisms. Read the length together with completeness and contamination.
  column: total_length
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Bins by phylum
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of bins with a GTDB-Tk phylum and the bars rank the phyla by their number of bins. It answers which lineages dominate the recovered genomes.
    How to read: a ranking led by one phylum means a community dominated by it. Bins without a phylum were not classified and are left out.
  column: bin_id
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: phylum
  top_n_count: 5
  filter_expr: col('phylum') != ''
  caption: bins, by phylum

- component: card
  title: Best bin quality score
  description: |-
    The hero number is the highest quality score of any bin, completeness minus five times contamination, and the bars rank the assemblers by their best bin. It answers which assembler produced the best genome.
    How to read: a tall bar for an assembler means it recovered at least one clean, complete bin. The median and minimum beside it show how the typical bin compares. The score is this table's own summary, not a published standard.
  column: quality_score
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  - min
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: assembler
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: best score, by assembler

- component: card
  title: Evidence per bin
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average count of the four tools (CheckM2, QUAST, Prokka and GTDB-Tk) that reported on each bin, and the histogram shows how bins spread over that count. It answers how complete the evidence behind each bin is.
    How to read: bins reported by fewer tools have blank columns in the table, so a low average means the MIMAG tier or lineage may be missing for some bins.
  column: sources_present
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: tools that reported, per bin

- component: table
  title: Bin summary
  description: |-
    One row is one recovered bin, with its completeness, contamination, assembly statistics, annotation counts, MIMAG tier and GTDB-Tk lineage. It answers whether an individual bin is good enough to use.
    How to read: Sort by completeness, highest first, then check the contamination and the MIMAG tier of the top rows. Look for bins with high completeness and low contamination, and for rows with a missing tier or lineage. It complements the quality and taxonomy tiles of the same output, which summarise these bins.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_vs_depth
  title: Contig length against depth
  description: |-
    Each point is a contig: its length on the horizontal axis and its read depth in one sample on the vertical axis, sized by its mean depth over all samples and coloured by the sample whose reads were mapped. It answers how coverage varies between contigs and between samples.
    How to read: contigs of one organism sit in a band of similar depth, which is the signal a binner uses. A contig deep in one sample and flat in another belongs to an organism only the first carries. Long contigs with very low depth may be poorly supported.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/mag. This catalog's recipe leaves contigs under 1 kbp out of the table, below the 1500 bp nf-core/mag uses by default as its minimum contig size for binning.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nf-core/mag/master/nextflow_schema.json
  kind: scatter_xy
  config:
    reference_line: horizontal
    reference_stat: median
    log_x: true
    x_title: Contig length (bp)
    y_title: Depth in this sample (X)
    top_n_labels: 0
    density_threshold: 5000
    legend_pos: bottom
  roles:
    x: contig_length
    y: depth
    label: contig_id
    color: read_sample
    size: mean_depth

- component: figure
  title: Contig depth distribution per sample
  description: |-
    Each bar counts the contigs in a range of depth, drawn per sample whose reads were mapped. It answers how deeply the assembly is covered in each sample.
    How to read: a sample whose histogram sits further right is more deeply sequenced. A large pile at zero means many contigs are absent from that sample, which is the differential coverage that separates organisms.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/mag.
  visu_type: histogram
  dict_kwargs:
    x: depth
    color: read_sample
    barmode: overlay
    labels:
      depth: Depth (X)
      read_sample: Sample
  reference_lines:
  - axis: x
    stat: median
    column: depth

- component: figure
  title: Contig depth by assembly and sample
  description: |-
    Each box summarises the contig depths of one assembly in one sample whose reads were mapped. It answers how coverage compares between assemblies and samples.
    How to read: boxes at similar heights mean comparable coverage. An assembly with a much lower box in one sample is poorly represented in that sample, and a wide box means a mix of abundant and rare organisms.
    Lines and annotations: the dashed line is the median depth of this table, a reference computed from the rows on show (it follows the filters), not a cut-off of nf-core/mag.
  visu_type: box
  dict_kwargs:
    x: assembly_id
    y: depth
    color: read_sample
    labels:
      assembly_id: Assembly
      depth: Depth (X)
      read_sample: Sample
  reference_lines:
  - axis: y
    stat: median
    column: depth

- component: card
  title: Contig depth
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median read depth of the contigs and the box shows the quartiles. It answers how deeply a typical contig is covered.
    How to read: a very low median means the reads barely cover the assembly and binning will be unreliable. A long upper tail holds highly abundant organisms.
  column: depth
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Longest contig
  description: |-
    The hero number is the length of the longest contig and the bars rank the assemblers by their longest contig. It answers how contiguous each assembly is.
    How to read: a longer contig means fewer breaks, which helps binning and annotation. The median beside it shows the typical contig, which is usually much shorter.
  column: contig_length
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: assembler
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: longest contig, by assembler

- component: card
  title: Contigs
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct contigs above the length floor, with the number of contig and sample rows beside it, and the bars rank the assemblers by their contigs. It answers how large the assemblies are.
    How to read: many more contigs from one assembler means it split the assembly into more pieces, or kept more short sequences.
  column: contig_id
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: assembler
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: contigs, by assembler

- component: card
  title: Mean depth over samples
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average of the contigs' mean depth over all samples, and the histogram shows how contigs spread over it. It answers how abundant contigs are overall, before the per-sample split.
    How to read: a long tail of high values means a few very abundant organisms hold most of the reads.
  column: mean_depth
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: mean depth, with its spread

- component: table
  title: Contig coverage
  description: |-
    One row is one contig in one sample whose reads were mapped, with the contig length, its mean depth, its depth in that sample and the variance. It answers which contigs hold the reads of which sample.
    How to read: Sort by the depth in that sample to find the contigs that dominate it, or by the variance to find uneven coverage. Look for long contigs with a low depth and short ones with a very high depth. It complements the depth tiles of the same output, which summarise these rows.

    How to read: a very low median means the reads barely cover the assembly and binning will be unreliable. A long upper tail holds highly abundant organisms.
  column: depth
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: card
  title: Longest contig
  description: |-
    The hero number is the length of the longest contig and the bars rank the assemblers by their longest contig. It answers how contiguous each assembly is.
    How to read: a longer contig means fewer breaks, which helps binning and annotation. The median beside it shows the typical contig, which is usually much shorter.
  column: contig_length
  aggregation: max
  aggregations:
  - median
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: assembler
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: longest contig, by assembler

- component: card
  title: Contigs
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of distinct contigs above the length floor, with the number of contig and sample rows beside it, and the bars rank the assemblers by their contigs. It answers how large the assemblies are.
    How to read: many more contigs from one assembler means it split the assembly into more pieces, or kept more short sequences.
  column: contig_id
  aggregation: nunique
  aggregations:
  - count
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: assembler
  top_n_count: 4
  caption: contigs, by assembler

- component: card
  title: Mean depth over samples
  description: |-
    The hero number is the average of the contigs' mean depth over all samples, and the histogram shows how contigs spread over it. It answers how abundant contigs are overall, before the per-sample split.
    How to read: a long tail of high values means a few very abundant organisms hold most of the reads.
  column: mean_depth
  aggregation: average
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: mean depth, with its spread

- component: table
  title: Contig coverage
  description: |-
    One row is one contig in one sample whose reads were mapped, with the contig length, its mean depth, its depth in that sample and the variance. It answers which contigs hold the reads of which sample.
    How to read: Sort by the depth in that sample to find the contigs that dominate it, or by the variance to find uneven coverage. Look for long contigs with a low depth and short ones with a very high depth. It complements the depth tiles of the same output, which summarise these rows.
